item.research_question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?
item.material_system: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure
item.processing_route: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method
item.test_conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K
key_findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).
Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).

Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.
Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.
Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.
Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.
The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.
item.mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.
item.limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.
item.future_work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.
quotes: This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces.
Specifically, the maximum strength of the pillar with a pre-existing twin exceeded 2.5 GPa, that is, about 1 GPa higher than that without a twin.

The dislocations moved fast along the boundaries, which is consistent with previous reports that demonstrated that the dislocation motion on a twin boundary would be faster than that in the matrix since the impediment from the image force is null if the Burgers vector of dislocations is parallel to the twin boundary.
